COMMUNITY SOLAR FARM LIGHTS UP MOUNTAIN VILLAGE

Last spring, the mountain village of Fuxing turned on its first community solar farm. For years, families there paid high prices for electricity because the nearest power line was far away, and storms often cut the supply for days.

The new solar farm was built on an old rice field that no farmer wanted to use anymore. Two hundred solar panels now cover the field, and the electricity goes straight into the village's small power grid. Villagers do not need to buy panels for their own roofs. Instead, everyone shares the power and the cost together.

The project cost about six million dollars. Half of the money came from the government, and half came from a private company that builds solar farms. In return, the company will look after the panels for twenty years and share part of the profit with the village.

Local leader Chen Mei-hua said the farm has already lowered electricity bills by nearly thirty percent. "We used to worry about blackouts every typhoon season," she said. "Now we make our own power, and we even sell the extra to the national grid."
stem: According to the passage, where was the solar farm built?
options: On the roof of the village's town hall building
On an old rice field that had been left unused
Beside the mountain road that connects Fuxing to the city
Next to the electricity company's regional office
explain_zh: 文中明確提到 solar farm 蓋在「no farmer wanted to use anymore」的舊稻田上，故答案為 B。選項 A 是說村民自己屋頂不用裝板，並非電廠位置；C、D 文章未提到，屬於憑空捏造的細節。細節題要直接回文章找對應句子核對。

IS FOOD DELIVERY REALLY CONVENIENT FOR EVERYONE?

Food delivery apps have changed the way many Taiwanese people eat. With a few taps on a phone, a hot meal can arrive at the door in thirty minutes. For busy students and office workers, this convenience feels like a small miracle. But is the system as good as it looks?

Supporters argue that delivery apps help small restaurants survive. A noodle shop with only four tables can now serve hundreds of customers a day without adding seats. Riders also earn flexible income; many say they like choosing their own hours.

Critics, however, point to the human cost. Riders are usually paid per order, not by the hour, so they often rush through red lights or ride in heavy rain to finish more trips. Studies show that delivery riders have a higher accident rate than most other workers. Restaurants complain too: apps can take up to thirty percent of each order as commission, leaving little profit for small businesses.

The truth is probably somewhere in the middle. Food delivery has clearly created new opportunities, but without safer rules for riders and fairer fees for restaurants, the 'miracle' comes at a real price that someone else quietly pays.
stem: What is the main idea of this passage?
options: Food delivery apps should be banned because they are dangerous for riders
Food delivery brings real benefits but also causes problems that need fixing
Small restaurants can no longer survive without using delivery apps
Riders earn more money than most other part-time workers in Taiwan
explain_zh: 文章先講外送的好處，再講騎士與店家付出的代價，最後結論說真相在中間，需要更安全的規則與更公平的抽成，所以主旨是B。A、C 都過於極端，文章沒有主張禁止或說店家「無法生存」；D 文中未比較所得高低。主旨題要找能包含正反兩面的敘述。

BUBBLE TEA: TAIWAN'S SWEETEST INVENTION

If you walk down any street in Taiwan, you will probably pass a bubble tea shop within a few minutes. These small drink stands, often called 'hand-shaken tea' shops, sell iced tea mixed with milk, fruit, and chewy tapioca balls known as 'boba.' For visitors, trying a cup is almost as important as seeing a night market.

Bubble tea was invented in Taichung in the 1980s. According to one popular story, a tea shop owner added tapioca balls to her iced tea just for fun, and customers loved the new texture. The drink quickly spread across the island and later around the world.

Today, ordering bubble tea in Taiwan is its own small skill. Customers choose the type of tea, the amount of sugar, the amount of ice, and extra toppings such as pudding or grass jelly. Regular customers often have a favorite order memorised, like "half sugar, less ice."

For travellers, bubble tea shops are a cheap and easy way to experience local culture. A cup usually costs less than a light meal, and most shops are open late into the night. Whether you like it very sweet or barely sweet at all, there is a bubble tea combination made just for you.
stem: What is the main idea of this passage?
options: Bubble tea started in Taichung by accident and later became famous worldwide
Bubble tea is a uniquely Taiwanese drink that visitors can easily enjoy and customize
Night markets are more important than bubble tea shops for tourists visiting Taiwan
Bubble tea shops in Taiwan are more expensive than most other local restaurants
explain_zh: 文章介紹手搖飲的由來、點餐客製化，最後說對旅客而言是便宜又方便體驗在地文化的方式，B 最能涵蓋全文重點。A 只講起源，範圍太窄；C 文章只是「幾乎跟逛夜市一樣重要」，並非比較誰更重要；D 與文章「比正餐便宜」相反。主旨題要選能概括各段落的敘述。

OLD MERCHANT HOUSE REOPENS AFTER FIVE-YEAR REPAIR

A hundred-year-old merchant house in Tainan reopened to the public last month after five years of careful repair work. The building, known locally as the Lin family house, was built in 1921 by a sugar merchant and later used as a warehouse before being left empty for decades.

By the time restoration began, the roof had partly collapsed, and termites had eaten through many of the wooden beams. Engineers first had to make the structure safe before any repair could start. Craftsmen then rebuilt the roof using the same red tiles and wooden joints as the original design, based on old photographs kept by the family's descendants.

The project cost more than forty million dollars, most of it paid by the city government. Officials say saving old buildings like this one is not just about history; it also brings tourists and jobs to the neighbourhood. Since similar restoration projects opened nearby, several small cafés and craft shops have appeared on the same street.

Not everyone welcomed the plan at first. Some residents worried that restoration would raise rents and push out long-time shopkeepers. The city has promised to limit rent increases in the area, though some shop owners remain doubtful. For now, the Lin family house stands as a rare example of Tainan's sugar-trade past, open for visitors to explore each weekend.
stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Tainan's sugar trade ended because too many merchant houses were destroyed by termites
The city government refused to pay for repairing any old buildings in Tainan
A historic merchant house was carefully restored and now benefits the local area, despite some concerns
Local shopkeepers are moving out of Tainan because rents have already increased sharply
explain_zh: 文章敘述林家古厝從損壞到修復完成、帶來觀光與店家進駐，也提到居民對租金上漲的擔憂，C 最能概括整篇報導的重點。A、B、D 都是文章沒有提到或與事實相反的內容。主旨題要涵蓋修復過程與正反影響兩個面向。

WHY YOUNG ATHLETES GET INJURED MORE OFTEN THAN BEFORE

Doctors in Taiwan have noticed a rise in sports injuries among teenagers over the past ten years. Ankle sprains, knee pain, and stress fractures are now common complaints at school health clinics, especially among students who play basketball or run track.

One major reason is specialization. In the past, students often played several different sports through the year. Today, many focus on a single sport from an early age, training the same muscles and joints again and again without enough rest. Sports doctors call this 'overuse injury,' and it happens when the body does not have time to recover between practices.

Experts recommend several simple changes. First, young athletes should try more than one sport to use different muscle groups. Second, coaches should build in rest days, since muscles actually grow stronger during recovery, not during training itself. Third, schools should set aside enough time for a full warm-up before every practice session.

With these changes, doctors believe injury rates among student athletes could drop significantly within just a few years.

WHY FALSE NEWS SPREADS FASTER THAN THE TRUTH

Every day, thousands of rumours circulate on social media in Taiwan, from fake health cures to invented political scandals. Researchers who study online behaviour have found something surprising: false stories usually spread faster and reach more people than accurate ones.

One reason is emotion. False stories are often written to shock or frighten readers, and people are more likely to share something that makes them feel surprised or angry. A calm, accurate news report rarely creates the same reaction.

Another reason is novelty. Rumours tend to describe something new or unusual, while real news often confirms what people already expect. Since human attention is naturally drawn to new information, strange claims get shared again and again before anyone checks whether they are true.

Fact-checking organisations try to slow this process down. In Taiwan, several groups now respond quickly to viral rumours, publishing clear explanations within hours. Some social media platforms also add warning labels to posts that have been proven false.

Still, experts warn that fact-checking alone cannot solve the problem. By the time a rumour is corrected, it has often already been seen by far more people than the correction ever reaches. Readers, they argue, must also learn to pause and question surprising claims before sharing them.

Accurate news reports always spread faster than false or invented stories online

DRONES TAKE OVER THE RICE FIELDS

On a farm in Yunlin County, a small drone rises above a rice field early in the morning. Instead of a farmer walking through mud with a heavy tank of fertiliser on his back, the drone flies a fixed pattern over the crop, spraying a fine mist below. The whole field, once a half-day job, is finished in fifteen minutes.

Agricultural drones like this one carry small tanks of fertiliser or pesticide and follow a route planned by GPS on a mobile app. Sensors on the drone measure how green the leaves are, which helps farmers see which parts of the field need more nutrients and which parts are already healthy. This targeted spraying uses less chemical overall than spraying the whole field evenly.

Farmers who have switched to drones say the biggest benefit is not speed but safety. Handling chemical sprays by hand for hours can cause skin and breathing problems over time, especially for older farmers. A drone keeps the operator standing well away from the spray.

The technology is not perfect. Drones can only fly for about twenty minutes before their batteries need changing, and strong wind can blow the spray off course. Even so, as prices fall, more small farms across Taiwan are expected to adopt drone spraying within the next few years.

The number of hours a farmer has spent working that day

THE FORMOSAN BLACK BEAR: TAIWAN'S SHY MOUNTAIN GUARDIAN

Deep in Taiwan's central mountains lives an animal found nowhere else in the world: the Formosan black bear. Easily recognised by the pale, V-shaped mark on its chest, this subspecies has become an unofficial symbol of Taiwan's wild forests, appearing on hiking gear, coins, and conservation posters.

Despite its fame, the bear is rarely seen. Formosan black bears are naturally shy and avoid contact with humans whenever possible. Bears caught in leg traps sometimes lose a paw, which can be fatal if they cannot hunt or climb properly afterward.

Camera traps placed deep in the mountains have recently captured rare footage of mother bears with cubs, a hopeful sign for researchers. Still, experts caution that recovery will take decades. Protecting enough connected forest for the bears to roam safely remains the single biggest challenge for Taiwan's conservation efforts.

NEW MOON MISSION AIMS TO TEST TECHNOLOGY FOR FUTURE ASTRONAUTS

An unmanned spacecraft launched successfully last week as part of a mission designed to test technology that future astronauts will need for longer stays on the Moon. Unlike earlier missions that focused mainly on landing and returning quickly, this mission will keep the spacecraft in lunar orbit for several months.

The spacecraft carries instruments to measure radiation levels, test a new type of solar panel, and trial a communication system that could allow astronauts to stay in contact with Earth even from the Moon's far side, an area that normally blocks direct signals.

Mission scientists say radiation is one of the biggest unknowns for long-term lunar missions. Without Earth's protective atmosphere, astronauts on the Moon would be exposed to far higher levels of cosmic radiation, so understanding exact exposure levels is essential before any crewed mission attempts an extended stay.

If the instruments perform well, engineers plan to include similar technology on a crewed mission expected later this decade, when astronauts hope to build a small research station near the Moon's south pole, where scientists believe frozen water may exist beneath the surface.

For now, the current mission has no crew aboard, reducing risk while still gathering data that will shape how future astronauts prepare for life beyond Earth.

The spacecraft carries instruments to measure radiation levels, test a new type of solar panel, and trial a communication system that could allow astronauts to stay in contact with Earth even from the Moon's far side, an area that normally blocks direct signals.

Mission scientists say radiation is one of the biggest unknowns for long-term lunar missions. Without Earth's protective atmosphere, astronauts on the Moon would be exposed to far higher levels of cosmic radiation, so understanding exact exposure levels is essential before any crewed mission attempts an extended stay.

If the instruments perform well, engineers plan to include similar technology on a crewed mission expected later this decade, when astronauts hope to build a small research station near the Moon's south pole, where scientists believe frozen water may exist beneath the surface.

For now, the current mission has no crew aboard, reducing risk while still gathering data that will shape how future astronauts prepare for life beyond Earth.
